overview.body:
**Ratatoskr** (*ratatoskr*) — Squirrel of Yggdrasil · Drill-tooth — is the squirrel of the world-ash [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]]: the small, tireless runner who bears the eagle's words down from the crown of the tree and carries Níðhǫggr's answers back up from the roots, keeping the feud between the top and the bottom of the cosmos supplied with fresh insults.[^1]

His attestation is as narrow as his road is long. One stanza of the Poetic Edda's *Grímnismál* names him and his office — ‘Ratatoskr is the squirrel who must run on Yggdrasill's ash; the eagle's words he must bear from above and tell to Níðhǫggr below’ — and one chapter of Snorri's *Gylfaginning* fills out the scene, adding the hawk Veðrfölnir between the eagle's eyes and naming the squirrel's cargo as *öfundarorð*, ‘malicious words’.[^1][^2] Nothing else in the Old Norse corpus mentions him.

The name is a compound: *rati*, ‘borer, auger’ — the very name of the gimlet [[odinn|Óðinn]] drives through the mountain in the mead-myth — and *toskr*, ‘tusk, tooth’, whence the standard gloss ‘drill-tooth’; a rival derivation from *rata*, ‘to travel, find one's way’, yields ‘travel-tooth’, and the dispute is genuinely open.[^3] PuniCodex restores the name as **Ratatoskr** — identical to the ASCII input, since normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in it — and the mechanical rule therefore places it in Tier 2. No domain is claimed: the plain-ASCII ratatoskr.com is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

sources.citation: Grímnismál 32 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 16, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).

Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. ratatoskr, toskr; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Ratatoskr** (nominative), a compound of two ordinary words. The second element is secure: *toskr*, ‘tusk, tooth’, cognate with Old English *tusc*. The first is the philologist's problem. The standard reading takes *rati*, ‘borer, auger’ — the name of the drill with which Óðinn bores into the mountain Hnitbjǫrg in the mead-of-poetry myth (*Hávamál* 106; *Skáldskaparmál*) — giving ‘drill-tooth’, a tooth that bores: exactly the instrument a squirrel carries in its face.[^1][^2]

The alternative derives the first element from the verb *rata*, ‘to travel, to find one's way’, yielding ‘travel-tooth’ — a derivation the handbooks register without settling, and one whose fit for the tireless courier of the world-tree has tempted more than one commentator.[^3] What is not in dispute is the word-class: Ratatoskr is a mythological coinage, never an ordinary human anthroponym, and appears nowhere outside the two Eddic witnesses.

The ASCII form survives unchanged because normalized Old Norse writes the name in plain Latin letters; the Unicode restoration **Ratatoskr** differs from the input only by its capital. Because the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no vowel length — the name is classified Tier 2, a statement about orthography and never about the creature.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **r** → **R** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **t** → **t** — Same
- **o** → **o** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **k** → **k** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name: the plain-ASCII **ratatoskr.com** is registered outside the collection and watched for release, and this temple stands without an address of its own.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈrɑ.tɑ.toskr/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Ra-** — Trilled [r], short open [ɑ]; the stress falls here, on the first syllable, as in every Old Norse word
- **-ta-** — Voiceless dental stop [t], short open [ɑ]
- **-toskr** — Voiceless stop [t], short rounded [o], then the cluster [skr]: sibilant, velar stop, and the final nominative [r], lightly syllabic as in modern Icelandic

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘RAH-tah-toskr’ — three even beats with the weight on the first, all vowels clipped short, and the final -r sounded as a light trill, as in Icelandic Ratatoskur.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Ratatoskr, the íkorni (squirrel) of the world-ash
- **Name elements** — *rati* ‘borer, auger’ (Óðinn's gimlet) + *toskr* ‘tusk, tooth’ (cf. Old English *tusc*)[^2]
- **Younger Futhark** — ᚱᛅᛏᛅᛏᚢᛋᚴᛦ, the normalized Viking-Age runic rendering (reconstructed; unattested)
- **Modern Icelandic** — Ratatoskur, the living form
- **Owned form** — none; the temple claims no domain

Ratatoskr is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII alphabet cannot write: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no length mark. The name travels from manuscript to address bar without losing a single feature — the tier rule records that fact mechanically.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. ratatoskr, toskr.

domains.body:
**Ratatoskr** is the courier of the world-ash — the one creature in Yggdrasill's great menagerie defined by an errand rather than by appetite, and the only messenger in the corpus whose cargo is mischief itself.[^1]

### The World-Tree's Courier

Grímnismál sets him his route with the modal *skal* — he *must* run: from the eagle in the crown to Níðhǫggr at the root, the full height of the cosmos in a squirrel's stride.[^1]

### Mischief

Snorri names the cargo: *öfundarorð*, ‘words of malice’ — the slander-tidings that keep the eagle above and the dragon below forever at enmity.[^2]

### The Vertical Axis

His road is the trunk of [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]] itself, the axis on which the Nine Worlds hang; no other creature in the Edda is given the whole height of the universe as a daily commute.[^2]

### The Tree's Menagerie

He runs in company: the unnamed eagle and the hawk Veðrfölnir above, the four harts in the branches, the serpents and Níðhǫggr beneath the roots in [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] — a household of gnawers and watchers among whom the squirrel alone speaks.[^1][^2]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 32-35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 15-16, trans. Faulkes (1987).

symbols.body:
Ratatoskr's iconography is fixed by two passages and nothing else — but those passages equip him completely:[^1]

- **The world-ash** — Yggdrasill, ‘the greatest and best of all trees’: his road, his world, and the axis of everyone else's[^2]
- **The malicious message** — *öfundarorð*, Snorri's exact word for the cargo: not news but malice, carried between powers too proud to speak directly[^1]
- **The drill-tooth** — the name itself, *rati* + *toskr*: the boring auger and the tusk, a tooth that drills and a tongue that bores[^3]
- **The hawk between the eyes** — Veðrfölnir, perched in the eagle's brow above the squirrel's route: the unblinking audit over every errand[^1]
- **The four harts** — Dáinn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr, Duraþrór, biting the buds of the ash he runs: the tree's other tenants, eaters where he is a talker[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 16, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Yggdrasill.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. ratatoskr, toskr.

mythology.body:
Ratatoskr's mythology is two passages long — one stanza and one prose chapter — and it is complete: a road, a cargo, a character. No saga, þula, or skaldic verse adds a word to him.

### The Squirrel's Stanza (Grímnismál 32)

In Grímnismál, [[odinn|Óðinn]] — masked as Grímnir and bound between the fires of King Geirrøðr — recites the inhabitants of the world-ash, and the squirrel receives his stanza: Ratatoskr is the íkorni who must run on Yggdrasill's ash; the eagle's words he must bear from above and tell to Níðhǫggr below. The verb is *skal*, ‘shall, must’: the running is an office, written into the tree's economy as fixedly as the dew that falls from its branches.[^1]

### The Suffering Ash (Grímnismál 33-35)

The surrounding stanzas build the tree's full menagerie and its misery. Four harts bite the new shoots; more serpents lie beneath the ash than any unwise ape would think — Góinn and Móinn, Grábakr and Grafvölluðr, Ófnir and Sváfnir — and gnaw the roots forever. Then the poem's most famous sentence: the ash of Yggdrasill suffers agony more than men know — the hart bites from above, the trunk rots at the side, and Níðhǫggr gnaws from below. Ratatoskr runs his messages through a tree being eaten alive at every level.[^1]

### Malice Up and Down the Trunk (Gylfaginning 16)

Snorri fills the stanza into a portrait. An eagle sits in the limbs of the ash and has knowledge of many things, and between its eyes sits a hawk called Veðrfölnir; the squirrel called Ratatoskr springs up and down the ash and bears *öfundarorð* — words of malice — between the eagle and Níðhǫggr. Where Grímnismál described a messenger, Snorri describes an agent provocateur: the squirrel does not merely deliver the correspondence of crown and root, he keeps the feud alive.[^2]

### The Dragon at the Root (Gylfaginning 15 · Völuspá 66)

The lower terminus of the squirrel's road is the worst address in the cosmos: the third root of the ash, over [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] and the spring Hvergelmir, where Níðhǫggr gnaws from below among countless serpents.[^2] Völuspá gives the Malice-Striker his other aspect — sucking the corpses of the dead at Nástrǫnd, and rising at last from Niðafjǫll with dead men on his wings — so that every word Ratatoskr carries down lands in the ear of the world's undertaker, and every word he carries up rises from it.[^3]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 32-35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 15-16, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Völuspá 66 and the Nástrǫnd stanzas (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

syncretism.body:
Ratatoskr belongs to a configuration far older and wider than Iceland: the world-tree with an eagle in its crown and a serpent at its root. The famous ancient parallel is the Mesopotamian Etana legend, in which an eagle and a serpent dwell in a single great tree and their broken pact drives the plot — a resemblance noted by comparativists for over a century. No line of borrowing has ever been demonstrated, and the standard handbooks treat the eagle-and-serpent tree as a widely distributed motif rather than a loan into the North.[^1]

Within the Germanic world the squirrel has no counterpart at all: he is the Edda's own addition to the tree-menagerie, and the only member defined by speech. His nearest functional kin are [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s ravens Huginn and Muninn, who likewise range the world and return with words — but the ravens gather news, while Ratatoskr, on Snorri's telling, manufactures a feud.[^2] Related figures in the corpus include [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]] (the tree he runs), [[mimir|Mímir]] (whose well stands beneath another of the tree's roots), and [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]] (the pantheon's other great serpent, though bound in the sea and no correspondent of the dragon at the root).

sources.citation: Dalley, Stephanie, Myths from Mesopotamia (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1989), the Etana legend; Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Yggdrasill, Ratatoskr.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr, Huginn and Muninn.

cultural-legacy.body:
Ratatoskr's afterlife grew with the tree he runs. Padraic Colum's *The Children of Odin* (1920) carried the squirrel into English-language retellings, and every popular handbook of Norse myth since has kept him running up and down the ash.[^1] Twentieth- and twenty-first-century readings sharpened Snorri's hint into an emblem: the squirrel as the patron of the poisonous go-between — the forwarder of insults, the courier who keeps enemies supplied — a role that has only gained force in the age of the forwarded message.

He has become a minor star of games and popular culture: a playable god in *Smite* (2015), and the scene-stealing squirrel of *God of War Ragnarök* (2022), where the ancient slander-courier is played, faithfully to Snorri, as the most insulting creature in the Nine Realms. In Iceland the name lives on as Ratatoskur, and modern Heathen and Ásatrú retellings keep him as the comic-dark emblem of how small tongues keep great hatreds fed.[^2]

sources.citation: Colum, Padraic, The Children of Odin: The Book of Northern Myths (New York: Macmillan, 1920).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr (on the figure's reception and interpretive history).

archaeology.body:
Ratatoskr is an entirely textual creature: no picture stone, runestone, amulet, or toponym preserves him, and the squirrel is otherwise invisible in Norse material culture.[^1] His two attestations hang on the great codices. Grímnismál survives in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), and Gylfaginning in the early fourteenth-century Codex Regius of the Prose Edda and its sister manuscripts, with the Grímnismál stanzas on the world-ash also copied into the Codex Wormianus and the Uppsala Edda tradition.[^2]

The world-ash itself has material echoes — the animal-and-tree compositions of Scandinavian and Insular art are sometimes compared to Yggdrasill's menagerie — but none can be tied to the squirrel by name. His evidence is the manuscript page alone, which is fitting for a figure made entirely of words.[^1]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr.

Larrington, Carolyne, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), introduction and note on Grímnismál; Faulkes, Anthony, Edda: Prologue and Gylfaginning (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982), manuscript history.

meditation.body:
Ratatoskr is the Edda's smallest cosmological fact and one of its sharpest. The universe is held in a tree; the tree is being eaten from crown to root; and through the middle of the disaster runs a squirrel, up and down, carrying the worst things the top and the bottom can think of to say to each other.[^1]

Snorri's word for the cargo is exact: *öfundarorð* — not news, not warnings, but malice. The myth knows something the etiquette books miss: that feuds do not survive on hatred alone but on delivery — that between every great enmity runs some small, quick, indispensable creature who keeps the words fresh. Ratatoskr never fights, never schemes on his own account, never speaks a line the sources record. He only carries. And the Edda gives him eternity for it: while the ash stands, the squirrel runs, and the eagle and the dragon never lack for ammunition.[^2]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 32-35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 16, trans. Faulkes (1987).

poetic-edda.body:
The Poetic Edda owns Ratatoskr outright: his one stanza is Grímnismál 32, spoken by the masked [[odinn|Óðinn]] in the catalogue of the world-ash's inhabitants. ‘Ratatoskr is the squirrel who must run on Yggdrasill's ash; the eagle's words he must bear from above and tell to Níðhǫggr below’ — the modal *skal* makes the running an office, not a habit.[^1]

The stanzas that frame him matter as much as his own. Grímnismál 33 names the four harts that bite the shoots; 34 counts the serpents beneath the ash — more than any unwise ape would think — and 35 delivers the poem's most famous sentence: the ash suffers agony, the hart bites from above, the trunk rots at the side, Níðhǫggr gnaws from below. The squirrel is the only member of this menagerie who carries anything.[^1]

Elsewhere the Edda supplies his name's raw material and his correspondent's dossier. *Hávamál* 106 names Rati, the auger Óðinn drives through the mountain for the mead of poetry — the first element of ‘drill-tooth’.[^2] And *Völuspá* gives Níðhǫggr his full horror: sucking corpses at Nástrǫnd, and at the end rising from Niðafjǫll with dead men on his wings — the ear into which the squirrel has poured the eagle's words for all time.[^3]

sources.citation: Grímnismál 32-35 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Hávamál 106 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Völuspá, the Nástrǫnd stanzas and stanza 66 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

prose-edda.body:
The Prose Edda is the squirrel's portraitist. Gylfaginning 16 turns Grímnismál's bare stanza into a scene: an eagle sits in the limbs of the ash and has knowledge of many things; between its eyes sits the hawk Veðrfölnir; and the squirrel called Ratatoskr springs up and down the ash and bears *öfundarorð* — words of malice — between the eagle and Níðhǫggr. Four harts, named there as Dáinn, Dvalinn, Duneyrr and Duraþrór, run among the branches and bite the buds.[^1]

Snorri's contribution is the single word that defines the figure: *öfundarorð*. Grímnismál's squirrel is a messenger; Snorri's is an instigator, a courier whose deliveries exist to keep crown and root at war. Interpreters have long debated how much of this is Snorri's own sharpening of the stanza — the poem says only that the eagle's words are carried down — but the slander-reading has governed the figure's whole afterlife, from the handbooks to the games.[^2] Gylfaginning 15 supplies the geography of his road: the three roots of the ash over Asgardr, Jǫtunheimr and [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]], the wells Urðarbrunnr, Mímisbrunnr and Hvergelmir beneath them, and Níðhǫggr gnawing the Niflheimr root from below.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 15-16, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr.

runic-evidence.body:
The runic corpus is silent on Ratatoskr, and the silence is expected: the name is a mythological coinage attested only in the two Eddic witnesses, never an anthroponym, and no stone, amulet, or graffito yet found carves it.[^1] In this he differs from the great gods, whose names or bynames surface in the epigraphic record; the squirrel belongs entirely to the world of the parchment page.

What the runes can supply is a normalized rendering. In the sixteen-rune Younger Futhark of the Viking Age the name would have been carved **ᚱᛅᛏᛅᛏᚢᛋᚴᛦ** — transliterated r-a-t-a-t-u-s-k-R, with the ᚢ rune writing the short o and ᛦ carrying the final nominative -r. The rendering is a reconstruction in the standard convention, not an attestation: it shows only how the manuscript name maps onto the runic row, underspecifications and all.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), on the runic rows and their transliteration.

sagas.body:
Beyond the Eddas, the medieval record is empty, and it is worth saying plainly. Ratatoskr appears in no Íslendingasaga, no fornaldarsaga, no king's saga; Saxo Grammaticus, whose Gesta Danorum retells so much of the divine mythology in euhemerized form, has no squirrel at the world-tree; and the skaldic corpus never uses his name as a heiti or in a kenning.[^1] Even the þulur — the versified name-lists that preserve the Old Norse vocabulary of creatures — add nothing to his dossier beyond the Grímnismál stanza some of them copy.

The absence is itself the datum. Ratatoskr is a cosmographic figure, not a narrative one: he exists to populate a description of the universe's plumbing, and once the description was given, the tradition never asked him to do anything else. His entire story is the office Grímnismál assigns him — run, bear, tell — and the character Snorri reads into it. Everything after, from Colum's children's book to the modern games, is reception of those two passages and no more.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Ratatoskr.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Ratatoskr.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Ratatoskr** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Grímnismál) and the early 14th-c. Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (Gylfaginning).[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives, so the manuscript form is the sole witness.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The compound is *rati* ‘borer, auger’ + *toskr* ‘tusk, tooth’, with the nominative singular ending *-r*.[^2]
- Old Norse orthography writes the name in nine plain Latin letters; no length marks or special characters occur.
- In the Younger Futhark the name maps to **ᚱᛅᛏᛅᛏᚢᛋᚴᛦ** (r-a-t-a-t-u-s-k-R): the ᚢ rune writes the short o, and ᛦ writes the final nominative -r — a normalized reconstruction, not an attested carving.[^3]
- The Unicode restoration Ratatoskr therefore differs from the ASCII form *ratatoskr* only by its capital; nothing distinctive is lost in transit, and the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule.

sources.citation: Larrington, Carolyne, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), note on Grímnismál; Faulkes, Anthony, Edda: Prologue and Gylfaginning (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1982), manuscript history.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. ratatoskr, toskr.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
